question: Should the state be able to refuse the name parents choose for a child?
answer: A name is imposed on someone who cannot object and follows them into every classroom. In 2008 a New Zealand court made a nine-year-old girl a ward of court so she could shed the name Talula Does The Hula From Hawaii. Registrars refusing a handful of names a year protect children at almost no cost.
move: Whichever side you took, it turns on who judges harm, and how often.
counterpoint: Naming is among the most personal choices a family makes, and officials are poor judges of what will embarrass. Iceland's naming committee rejected Blær as a boy's name; in 2013 the girl given it won a court case to keep her name, after years registered simply as Stúlka, girl. Rules made for oddities end up policing ordinary families.
reference: Personal Names Act No. 45/1996 (Lög um mannanöfn), Althingi, Iceland, 1996
